主要内容: Intel (INTC) reported its third-quarter earnings on October 21, 2021, revealing a decline in PC chip sales due to industry-wide component shortages. The company attributed the 2% shrinkage in its PC chip business to reduced laptop volumes and a lack of other parts needed for assembling computers. Intel also warned that its gross margin and free cash flow would decline over the next two to three years due to increased capital expenditure, including a $20 billion investment in new chip factories and a semiconductor foundry in Arizona. Despite the challenges, Intel's Data Center Group saw a 10% year-over-year revenue increase to $6.5 billion, driven by demand for on-premise servers. CEO Pat Gelsinger stated that PC demand remains strong, though the semiconductor shortage is expected to persist until 2023. Analysts suggest the pandemic-driven PC surge may be waning, but Gelsinger believes the PC business is now structurally larger, with daily sales reaching a million units. Intel reported a gross margin of 56% for Q3 2021, up 2.9% year-over-year. The company plans to transition into a foundry business, manufacturing chips for other designers, in addition to its own processors. This shift is expected to be costly but could benefit from government support in the U.S. and Europe. Intel also noted growth in its internet of things group, which increased 54% to $1 billion, and Mobileye, its automotive chip subsidiary, which grew 39% to $326 million. Intel's CFO, George Davis, announced his retirement in May 2022. The company will provide more details on its foundry transition and technology roadmap at its analyst day in February 2022.
